title: A runtime operator's name and kind come from their credential, not the request body
statement: With OPERATOR_CREDENTIALS set, every /runtime write resolves its change-manager Actor from the operator secret alone: the matching credential supplies the name and the kind (human or ai), and a body whose operator or actor_kind disagrees is refused with 403, an unknown secret with 401, and a malformed or ambiguous credential map (shared secret, ai credential on OPERATOR_SECRET) with 503. Without it, the OPERATOR_SECRET holder is the human operator and actor_kind can only lower that to ai. Approval still needs no second person, so a solo human operator is not blocked.
failure_mode: actor_for built the Actor from the caller-chosen operator name and actor_kind, checked only against one shared OPERATOR_SECRET, so an AI client holding the secret sent actor_kind=human and became an approver of LIVE_GATED, SHADOW and CANARY changes, and the audit recorded whatever name it typed. ChangeManager.approve trusts the Actor's kind, and no test sent a kind that disagreed with the caller's identity; the deciding test now does, through actor_for and through the approve route.
notes: Audit API-012 (option 2: credential-bound identity, no four-eyes rule). Requester != approver is deliberately not enforced so a single human operator can still approve. layer: test-suite
